subject: history
topic: How colonial borders reshaped the genetic landscape of modern nations
angle: While colonial history is linked to significant losses of genetic diversity in specific large mammal populations and is identified as a factor in human admixture and cognitive patterns, the sources do not provide a comprehensive map of how arbitrary borders specifically reshaped the genetic landscape of modern nations.
title: The Genetics of Colonial Borders

hooks.text: What does your biology say about colonial borders?
You see borders. The data shows genetic loss.
You ignore the biological cost of human history.
A line on a map and a loss of diversity.

reveal.headline: Colonialism left a genetic mark on southern African mammals.
reveal.body: The two southernmost populations of cape buffalo have significantly lower heterozygosity levels of 0.33% and 0.29% compared to the rest of the population. The evidence regarding how arbitrary borders specifically shaped national genetic landscapes is mixed or contested.

explain.headline: Human impacts reshaped the landscape.
explain.body: Human-mediated impacts during the colonial period caused massive losses of large mammal abundance in southern africa. Genetic data shows a link to historical mixture events caused by european colonialism.

matters.headline: The past is written in biology.
matters.body: That may be why we see patterns of diversity and mixture in modern populations. History is not just a series of dates. It is a physical reality in our genetic data.

example.headline: A map on a dusty wall.
example.body: You look at a map of africa. You see straight lines. You do not see the genetic diversity that was lost when those lines were drawn.

question.headline: What other histories are hidden in your own biology?

claims.text: Religion, a history of colonialism, and a history of Communist rule are important in some cases regarding the worldwide patterns of cognitive test performance.
claims.quote: Religion, a history of colonialism, and a history of Communist rule are important in some cases.

claims.text: Events across the past three centuries were the main drivers of the exceptional loss of genetic diversity in the southernmost populations of Cape buffalo, which coincided with the onset of colonialism.
claims.quote: detailed investigations of recent demographic history show that events across the past three centuries were the main drivers of the exceptional loss of genetic diversity in the southernmost populations, coincident with the onset of colonialism in the southern extreme of the Cape buffalo range.

claims.text: Genetic data alone can be used to identify historical mixture events, including those caused by European colonialism.
claims.quote: We identified events whose dates and participants suggest they describe genetic impacts of the Mongol empire, Arab slave trade, Bantu expansion, first millennium CE migrations in Eastern Europe, and European colonialism

claims.text: The two southernmost populations of Cape buffalo have significantly lower heterozygosity levels of 0.33% and 0.29% compared to the rest of the population.
claims.quote: with the two southernmost populations having significantly lower heterozygosity levels (0. 33% and 0. 29%) on par with that of the domesticated water buffalo (0. 29%).

claims.quote: our results add to the growing body of studies suggesting that multiple recent human-mediated impacts during the colonial period caused massive losses of large mammal abundance in southern Africa.

verdict: The evidence shows that colonial-era human impacts caused specific genetic diversity losses in southern African mammals and are detectable in human admixture history, but it does not provide a broad analysis of national border effects.
caveat: The sources focus on specific species, regions, or historical events rather than providing a systematic analysis of how arbitrary colonial borders specifically defined the genetic landscapes of modern nations.
caption:
Colonial history leaves physical traces on the natural world. 

Research shows that human-mediated impacts during the colonial period caused massive losses of large mammal abundance in southern africa. However, the evidence does not provide a comprehensive map of how arbitrary borders specifically reshaped the genetic landscape of modern nations. 

How does knowing this change your view of the map?
